blocks: Table 3: This table presents items (a) through (q), which constitute the definition of an “anti-gun” bill. Following
analysis of the bills returned in the Congress.gov search, these various clauses were determined to be relevant aspects
of legislation that seeks to curtail access to firearms or expand existing restrictions on firearms. In the same fashion as
the pro-gun clauses in Table 2, items (a) through (r) served as the guiding definitions for the “anti-gun” coding in this
study. An example of an “anti-gun” bill is S. 641, which is the Handgun Control and Violence Prevention Act of 1995,
proposed in the 104th Congress. This bill would “amend the Federal criminal code to prohibit the sale, delivery, or
other transfer of a handgun to an individual not possessing a valid Federal firearms license” and would “prohibit the
sale, delivery, or other transfer of handgun ammunition to an individual not possessing a Federal firearms license.”
These two provisions fit clause (a) in Table 3, and thus S. 641 was coded as an “anti-gun” bill.
Table 4: Items (a) through (d) in the table above include gun-related clauses frequently seen in the bills generated by
the Congress.gov search that were deemed not applicable to the coding guidelines developed above. For instance, item
(a) discusses military use of weapons, which has no applicability to civilian firearm use or domestic gun violence.
Further, items (b) and (d) are clauses that are not specific enough to be coded as either pro-gun or anti-gun. Item (c)
relates tangentially to gun legislation because it provides for consideration of such legislation, but it does not
specifically increase or decrease restrictions on firearms.
